title: Reading Job Postings — What Do They Require?
description: Learn to read and understand job postings and ask about requirements
objectives: Read and understand a simple job posting
Ask about job requirements you do not understand
Say whether you meet a requirement or not

phrases: You need to [be able to lift 50 lbs]
Do I have to [have a diploma]?
I don't have that yet, but I'm working on it
target_language.grammar_pattern:
MUST / NEED TO / HAVE TO (obligation)
  You must have a driver's license. (required — no exceptions)
  You need to pass a background check. (required step)
  Do I have to work weekends? (asking about requirement)

REQUIRED vs PREFERRED
  'Required' = you MUST have this — no exceptions.
  'Preferred' = it helps, but you can still apply without it.

SHOULD (advice, not obligation)
  You should bring a resume. (good idea, not required)

grammar_patterns.label: MUST for requirements
grammar_patterns.pattern: You must + [base verb] / You must have + [noun]
examples: You must be 18 years or older.
You must have a valid ID.
Applicants must speak English.
You must be able to lift 50 pounds.

grammar_patterns.label: NEED TO for steps
examples: You need to fill out an application.
You need to pass a drug test.
Do I need to have a resume?
You don't need to have a degree for this job.

grammar_patterns.label: DO I HAVE TO for questions
examples: Do I have to work on weekends?
Do I have to have a high school diploma?
Do I have to bring anything to the interview?
Do I have to speak perfect English?

story.context: Ahmed finds a job posting at the community center. He asks his English teacher, Ms. Kim, to help him read and understand it.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: Ms. Kim, can you help me? I found a job, but I don't understand all the words.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Kim
dialogue.text: Of course! Let me see. It says: 'Warehouse Associate — Full Time. $18/hour.' What part is confusing?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: Here it says 'required' and here it says 'preferred.' What is the difference?

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Kim
dialogue.text: Good question. 'Required' means you must have it — no exceptions. 'Preferred' means it helps, but you can still apply without it.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: Okay. So it says a driver's license is required. I don't have a U.S. license yet.

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Kim
dialogue.text: Then you cannot apply for that position. But look here — this other posting says a license is only preferred.

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: Oh! And it says 'must be able to lift 50 pounds.' I can do that. And 'experience preferred, not required.' So I can apply?

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Kim
dialogue.text: Yes! You meet most of the requirements. Do you have any questions you want to ask the employer?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: Yes — do I have to work on weekends? And do I need to bring anything to the interview?

dialogue.speaker: Ms. Kim
dialogue.text: Those are excellent questions. You should also ask: is a background check required?

dialogue.speaker: Ahmed
dialogue.text: I understand now. 'Required' means I must have it. 'Preferred' means it helps but is not required. I can do this!

drills.title: Must and Need To
drills.instruction: Complete the requirement. Use: must / need to + [verb]

prompts.sentence: You ___ be 18 years or older to apply.
You ___ to fill out the application form online.
You ___ to bring two references to the interview.

examples: You must be able to lift heavy boxes.
You need to pass a background check.
You must have work authorization.
You need to complete a 3-day training.
Applicants must speak basic English.

drills.title: Do I Have To?
drills.instruction: Ask about requirements. Use: Do I have to + [verb]?

prompts.sentence: ___ I have to work on weekends?
___ I have to have a high school diploma?
___ we have to bring our own tools?

examples: Do I have to work nights?
Do I have to have a driver's license?
Does the job require weekends?
Do I have to bring anything to the interview?
Do I have to speak perfect English?
drills.your_turn: Do I have to speak perfect English?

drills.title: Required vs Preferred
drills.instruction: Listen and decide: is it required or preferred? Use the words in your answer.

prompts.sentence: A diploma is ___. You cannot apply without one.
Experience is ___. It helps, but you can still apply.
A background check is ___. Everyone must pass it.
Spanish is ___. It is useful but not necessary.

examples: A valid ID is required. You must have one.
A college degree is preferred but not required.
Lifting ability is required for this job.
Computer skills are preferred.
A driver's license is required for delivery jobs.
drills.your_turn: A driver's license is required for delivery jobs.

listening.question: According to the job posting, what is REQUIRED?
listening.transcript: Let's look at the job posting. Required: a valid ID and the ability to lift 50 pounds.
options: A college degree and Spanish
A valid ID and the ability to lift 50 pounds
A driver's license and 2 years of experience
A resume and a high school diploma
listening.explanation: The posting says 'Required: valid ID, ability to lift 50 lbs.' A degree, Spanish, and license are all listed as preferred or not mentioned.

listening.question: What does 'preferred but not required' mean for this position?
listening.transcript: The posting says experience is preferred but not required. That means you can apply without experience, but having it helps.
options: You must have experience to apply
Experience will get you a higher salary
You can apply without experience, but having it helps
The employer does not care about experience
listening.explanation: 'Preferred but not required' means the employer would like you to have experience, but they will still interview you without it. It is not a hard rule.

listening.question: What question does the man ask the employer?
listening.transcript: The man had one important question for the employer: Do I have to work on weekends?
options: Do I have to wear a uniform?
Do I have to work on weekends?
Do I need to bring a reference?
Does the job pay overtime?
listening.explanation: The man asks 'Do I have to work on weekends?' because he needs to know his schedule. This is one of the most common and important questions to ask an employer.

speaking.title: Reading a Job Posting Aloud
speaking.instruction: Look at this job posting and read it aloud clearly: 'Cashier needed. Must be 18+. Must be able to work weekends. Experience preferred but not required. Apply in person with a valid ID.' Then say in your own words what is required and what is preferred.
speaking.example: This job needs a cashier. You must be 18 years old or older. You must work on weekends — that is required. Experience helps, but you can apply without it. You need to bring a valid ID when you apply.

speaking.title: Ask Three Questions
speaking.instruction: Imagine you want to apply for a warehouse job. Record yourself asking the employer 3 questions about the requirements using: Do I have to...? Do I need to...? Is ... required?
speaking.example: Hello, I'm interested in the warehouse job. I have three questions. First, do I have to have a driver's license? Second, do I need to bring anything to the interview? And third, is a background check required? Thank you.

writing.title: Write a Job Requirement List
writing.instruction: Write 4 sentences describing the requirements for a job you know about (a store, restaurant, warehouse, school). Use: must, need to, required, preferred.
writing.example: To work at a restaurant, you must be at least 16 years old. You need to be able to stand for a long time. A food handler certificate is required in some states. Experience is preferred, but many restaurants will train you.

writing.title: Do You Meet the Requirements?
writing.instruction: Read this job posting: 'Driver needed. Must have a valid license. Must speak English. Lifting ability required. Computer skills preferred.' Write 4 sentences explaining which requirements you meet and which you don't have yet.
writing.example: I meet most of the requirements for this job. I have a driver's license and I can speak English. I can lift heavy things, so that requirement is not a problem. I do not have strong computer skills yet, but that is only preferred, not required. I am going to apply.

sections.title: MUST vs NEED TO — both mean required
examples: You must have a valid ID. = You need to have a valid ID.
You must be 18. = You need to be 18.
Applicants must speak English. = Applicants need to speak English.
BUT: 'must' sounds more official and strict.
'Need to' sounds more like a practical step.
sections.question: Are MUST and NEED TO different in meaning?
sections.explanation: MUST and NEED TO both express obligation — something that is required. However, MUST sounds more formal and strict (like a law or a firm rule), while NEED TO sounds more practical (like a step in a process). Job postings often use MUST. When asking questions, we usually use NEED TO or HAVE TO, not MUST.

sections.title: REQUIRED vs PREFERRED in job postings
examples: Required: Driver's license ← You MUST have this
Preferred: College degree ← Nice to have, not a must
Required: Ability to lift 50 lbs ← Non-negotiable
Preferred: Bilingual (Spanish) ← Helpful but optional
If you don't meet a REQUIRED item, don't apply.
If you don't meet a PREFERRED item, you can still apply.
sections.question: What is the practical difference between 'required' and 'preferred'?
sections.explanation: REQUIRED means the employer will not hire you without this qualification. PREFERRED means the employer would like it, but they will still consider your application without it. Always check carefully: if you are missing a REQUIRED qualification, your application will likely be rejected. Missing a PREFERRED qualification is usually acceptable.

quiz.question: A job posting says 'Driver's license required.' What does this mean?
options: A driver's license would be helpful
You must have a driver's license to apply
You can get a license after you start
A license is optional for this job
quiz.explanation: 'Required' means you must have it. You cannot apply for this job without a driver's license.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses MUST?
options: You must to have a valid ID.
You musts have a valid ID.
You must have a valid ID.
You must having a valid ID.
quiz.explanation: MUST is followed by the base verb — no 'to', no -s, no -ing. 'You must have' is correct.

quiz.question: How do you ask about a requirement politely?
options: Must I to work weekends?
Do I have to work weekends?
I must work weekends?
Have I to work weekends?
quiz.explanation: 'Do I have to + [verb]?' is the standard way to ask about requirements. It is natural, polite, and grammatically correct.

quiz.question: A job posting says 'Experience preferred.' Ahmed has no experience. What should he do?
options: He cannot apply for this job
He should apply — preferred is not required
He must get experience first
He should not mention his lack of experience
quiz.explanation: 'Preferred' means it helps but is not a requirement. Ahmed can still apply and may get the job, especially if his other skills are strong.

quiz.question: Which is the MOST important question to ask before applying?
options: What is the office phone number?
What color is the uniform?
What are the requirements for this position?
Who was the last person hired?
quiz.explanation: Before applying, always confirm you meet the requirements. This saves everyone time and shows professionalism.

quiz.question: What does 'You need to fill out an application' mean?
options: Filling out an application is optional
Filling out an application is required
The application is already complete
You need help with the application
quiz.explanation: 'Need to' means it is required — you must do it. 'You need to fill out an application' means this is a required step.

quiz.question: In the dialogue, what word did Ms. Kim use to describe 'required'?
options: Helpful
Optional
Preferred
Must have — no exceptions
quiz.explanation: Ms. Kim says 'Required means you must have it — no exceptions.' This is the clearest definition of a required qualification.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses SHOULD correctly?
options: You should to bring a resume.
You shoulds bring a resume.
You should bring a resume.
You should bringing a resume.
quiz.explanation: SHOULD, like CAN and MUST, is followed by the base verb. 'You should bring' is correct. SHOULD means it is a good idea (advice), not a hard requirement.

quiz.question: Write a 3-item list of requirements for an imaginary job. Use: must, required, and need to.
quiz.explanation: Practice writing job requirements the way real employers write them. Use at least one 'must', one 'required', and one 'need to'.

quiz.question: Read this requirement: 'Must be able to work Monday to Friday, 7 AM to 4 PM.' Can you do this? Write 2 sentences explaining your answer.
quiz.explanation: Connect real job requirements to your own availability. Saying clearly what you can and cannot do is an important skill.

somali.description: Baro sida loo akhriyo loona fahmo xayaysiisyada shaqada, shuruudahana loo waydiiyo
objectives: Akhri oo faham xayaysiis shaqo oo fudud
Waydii shuruudaha shaqada ee aadan fahmin
Sheeg inaad shuruud buuxinayso iyo in kale

sections.explanation: MUST iyo NEED TO labaduba waxay muujiyaan waajib — wax loo baahan yahay. Si kastaba, MUST waxay u dhawaaqdaa si rasmi iyo adag (sida sharci ama qaanuun adag), halka NEED TO ay u dhawaaqdo si wax-ku-ool ah (sida tallaabo hab-socod). Xayaysiisyada shaqadu inta badan waxay isticmaalaan MUST. Su'aalaha, waxaan caadi ahaan isticmaalnaa NEED TO ama HAVE TO, ma aha MUST.

REQUIRED waxay ka dhigan tahay in shaqo-bixiyuhu aanu ku shaqaalaysiin la'aanteed. PREFERRED waxay ka dhigan tahay in shaqo-bixiyuhu jeclaan lahaa, laakiin weli codsigaaga way tixgelin doonaan la'aanteed. Mar walba si taxaddar leh u hubi: haddii aad ka maqan tahay shuruud REQUIRED ah, codsigaaga waxay u badan tahay in la diido. Ka maqnaanshaha shuruud PREFERRED ah caadi ahaan waa la aqbali karaa.
